text.p: Brazil's Gustavo Kuerten ensured a carnival atmosphere at Roland Garros on Sunday after destroying Sergi Bruguera in straight sets to be crowned the most unlikely men's champion in French Open history.

The 20-year-old, who received a good luck fax from Brazilian soccer legend Pele before the final, tore the Spaniard's impressive clay reputation to shreds with a stunning 6-3 6-4 6-2 final victory which made him the first unseeded French winner since Mats Wilander in 1982.

After receiving the trophy from another sporting great, Sweden's Bjorn Borg who won a record six French titles, Kuerten danced on a balcony to a samba beat provided by some ecstatic compatriots on the concourse below before attempting to explain the most unexpected men's Grand Slam triumph in years.

"Before the match I thought I could have won, but I didn't think I could win in three sets and 6-2 in the third," laughed the Brazilian, ranked 66 in the world before the most remarkable fortnight of his life.
"Now it's mine and I think I deserved it because I had to fight. Today was a great day for tennis and sport in Brazil."

Kuerten, who with the possible exception of Andre Agassi stands among tennis history's most colourfully-dressed champions, will now vault straight into the top 20 after adding Bruguera to a list which already included former champions Yevgeny Kafelnikov and Thomas Muster.

Not since Boris Becker won Wimbledon in 1985 at the age of 17 has a player shot from obscurity in such dramatic fashion and Bruguera's two previous French titles in 1993 and 1994 proved no defence at all.
For a set and a half, the Spaniard saw only a blur of blue and yellow on the opposite side of the net as his agile opponent produced a marvellous array of winners to lead by a set and 3-1.

Kuerten then had to withstand a brief fightback from Bruguera, saving three break points to hold for 5-4, but the way he skipped back to his chair after that game correctly implied that victory was almost his.
"I felt so good out there," said Brazil's first male Grand Slam champion, who dedicated his triumph to his deceased father after completing victory in one hour 50 minutes.
"When I lost him I was just eight years old and I didn't expect to be a tennis player," he said. "This tournament goes to him."

The Brazilian was even polite enough to wipe his feet free of clay dust before going up to receive the trophy from Borg and the winning cheque for $695,500, more than double the amount he has earned in his career to date.

He has never won a senior title before and the final was only the 49th match of his professional career, but the staggering inventiveness and touch he showed against Bruguera suggested Brazil have a new champion to be proud of for years.
Parisian crowds appreciate style more than most but anything Kuerten may lack in terms of sartorial elegance, he more than makes up for with his daredevil spirit.

He also had the precious commodity of luck on his side and Bruguera's defeat might have been less crushing had the ball not bounced the Brazilian's way off the net-cord on crucial points early in both the second and third sets.
After his semifinal win over Belgian Filip Dewulf, Kuerten had joked that "Maybe God is from Brazil" but this was clearly a case of fortune favouring the brave.
Two of the sweetest drop-shots imaginable which helped establish the decisive break in the sixth game of the final set would have graced any contest and Bruguera had no complaints.
"I want to give him the credit," the Spaniard said. "I thought he played an outstanding match."
The Brazilian's win crowned an extraordinary tournament which also saw a surprise winner in the women's singles when Croatia's Iva Majoli defeated world number one Martina Hingis in Saturday's final.
